explanation: SET NOCOUNT OFF leaves DONE_IN_PROC row-count messages enabled, increasing network traffic and client overhead.
SET XACT_ABORT OFF allows runtime errors to leave transactions open or partially applied instead of automatically rolling back.
SELECT * from Sales.Orders couples callers to all current and future columns and prevents covering-index optimization.
SELECT TOP (10) from Sales.Orders without an ORDER BY clause returns an arbitrary, non-deterministic set of rows.
DISTINCT on Sales.Orders.OrderID is redundant because OrderID is already the primary key and guaranteed unique.
WITH (NOLOCK) on Sales.Orders reads uncommitted data and can cause dirty reads, missing rows, or duplicate rows.
Applying YEAR(o.OrderDate) in the WHERE clause prevents an index seek on OrderDate and forces a scan.
Comparing int column o.CustomerID to nvarchar variable @CustomerIdText forces implicit conversion and can prevent index seeks.
Using (@CustomerID IS NULL OR o.CustomerID = @CustomerID) hinders cardinality estimation and often forces a scan instead of a seek.
o.Comments LIKE N'%urgent%' starts with a leading wildcard, preventing index seeks and forcing a full scan.
NOT IN against a subquery on Sales.Invoices.CustomerID can return zero rows unexpectedly if any NULL value is produced.
Wrapping o.CustomerID in ISNULL(o.CustomerID, 0) makes the predicate non-sargable and prevents using the index on CustomerID.
Performing arithmetic (o.OrderID + 0) on the key column prevents a direct index seek on PK_Sales_Orders.
Inequality predicate o.CustomerID <> 1 is poorly selective and typically forces a broad index or table scan.
CROSS JOIN between Sales.Orders and Sales.Customers has no join predicate and produces a Cartesian product.
Comma-separated tables (Sales.Orders, Sales.OrderLines) with the join condition in WHERE use deprecated syntax and risk accidental cross joins.
Correlated scalar subquery counting Sales.OrderLines executes a separate lookup per row in Sales.Orders.
Correlated EXISTS subquery against Sales.OrderLines checks existence per outer row instead of using a set-based join.
The CASE expression on o.Comments is duplicated in both the SELECT list and the ORDER BY clause.
ORDER BY 2 relies on select-list column position, which breaks silently if columns are reordered or added.
OFFSET 0 ROWS FETCH NEXT 10 ROWS ONLY orders only by non-unique o.OrderDate without a unique tie-breaker such as o.OrderID.
UNION performs unnecessary duplicate removal between mutually exclusive branches (o.OrderID = 1 and o.OrderID = 2).
Using (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Sales.OrderLines ...) > 0 counts all matching rows instead of short-circuiting with EXISTS.
SELECT @OrderID = o.OrderID FROM Sales.Orders without filtering or ordering silently overwrites @OrderID with the last arbitrary row.
Table variable @OrderIds lacks distribution statistics and can cause poor cardinality estimates.
SELECT TOP (5) o.OrderID from Sales.Orders without an ORDER BY clause inserts an arbitrary set of rows into @OrderIds.
SELECT ... INTO #ImplicitOrders creates a temporary table implicitly and can hold schema locks during population.
Cursor order_cursor processes Sales.Orders row by row instead of using a set-based query.
WHILE @Counter <= 1 performs iterative procedural looping instead of set-based processing.
Dynamic SQL string is built by concatenating @CustomerID rather than using parameterized sp_executesql.
EXEC sys.sp_executesql @Sql executes concatenated SQL without binding @OrderID as a parameter, causing plan cache bloat.
Temporary table #Scratch is created explicitly but never dropped before the stored procedure ends.
CATCH block selects ERROR_MESSAGE() without rethrowing via THROW or returning an error status, silently swallowing the failure.
RAISERROR is used instead of the modern THROW statement for raising an error.
PRINT statement emits unstructured diagnostic text that is buffered and unsuitable for production logging.
Query hard-codes business identifier o.CustomerID = 1 directly in the predicate instead of using a parameter or lookup.
Unlabelled date literal '20160101' is embedded directly in the predicate on o.OrderDate.
CONVERT(date, '01/02/2016') omits an explicit style code and depends on session DATEFORMAT settings.
Applying COALESCE in the join predicate between Sales.Orders and Sales.Invoices prevents efficient index-based join strategies.
Sales.Orders is self-joined on OrderID = o2.OrderID only to select o.OrderID, which is already available without the join.
ORDER BY o.Comments sorts all rows of Sales.Orders by an nvarchar(MAX) LOB column.
SUM(ol.Quantity) aggregates the entire Sales.OrderLines table without any WHERE filter.
HAVING ol.OrderID > 0 filters individual rows after grouping instead of filtering in WHERE before aggregation.
ORDER BY OrderCount is redundant on a scalar aggregate query without GROUP BY that always returns a single row.
MERGE on Sales.Orders has known concurrency and correctness edge cases compared to separate UPDATE/INSERT statements.
UPDATE Sales.Orders SET Comments = Comments writes the same value back, generating unnecessary locking and transaction log activity.
DELETE FROM Sales.OrderLines WHERE Quantity = -1 uses a broad non-key predicate rather than a primary key.
WAITFOR DELAY '00:00:01' blocks a SQL Server worker thread unnecessarily.
BEGIN TRANSACTION is not enclosed in a TRY...CATCH block, risking unrolled-back open transactions on error.
SET IDENTITY_INSERT Sales.Orders ON alters session state and couples application code to explicit identity management.
EXEC sp_who invokes a system procedure without a schema qualifier.
SET ROWCOUNT 1 changes a session-level setting and never restores it to 0.
INSERT INTO #DemoCategories VALUES (...) omits an explicit column list, making it fragile to schema changes.
CustomerName LIKE '%' + @CustomerName + '%' uses a leading wildcard, preventing an index seek on UQ_Sales_Customers_CustomerName.
User parameter @CustomerName is concatenated directly into @sql before execution via sp_executesql, creating a SQL injection vulnerability.
UPDATE #DemoCustomers lacks a WHERE clause and will overwrite CustomerCategoryID for every row in the table.
WHERE o.OrderDate >= '2016-01-01' filters on the outer-joined table Sales.Orders, silently converting the LEFT JOIN into an INNER JOIN.
WHERE DeliveryMethodID = NULL always evaluates to UNKNOWN in T-SQL; use IS NULL instead.
Scalar UDF dbo.GetCustomerType(CustomerID) in the SELECT list forces row-by-row evaluation across Sales.Customers.
CATCH block handles an error inside an explicit transaction without rolling back, leaving the transaction open.
WITH (INDEX = 1) hardcodes an index ID on Sales.Customers, which can break or cause suboptimal plans if indexes change.
Query nests subqueries 3 levels deep (t1, t2, t3), reducing readability and hindering optimizer simplification.
CustomerName LIKE '%A%' uses a leading wildcard, preventing an index seek on Sales.Customers.CustomerName.
SELECT * from dbo.GetCustomerOrdersMulti couples callers to all columns returned by the function.
Query calls multi-statement TVF dbo.GetCustomerOrdersMulti, which prevents plan inlining and typically yields poor cardinality estimates.
